title: Docs: self-hosting cacheHandler example is an unbounded in-memory cache and disables the default LRU
body:
### What is the documentation issue?

The `cache-handler.js` example in [Self-Hosting → Configuring Caching](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/self-hosting#configuring-caching) stores entries in a module-level `Map` with no size limit, no TTL, and no eviction. The paired `next.config.js` also sets `cacheMaxMemorySize: 0`.

As written, the example:

1. **Grows memory without bound.** Entries are removed only by `revalidateTag`. ISR pages per path and `fetch` entries with high-cardinality keys (query strings, dynamic params) accumulate until the process is OOM-killed.
2. **Is worse than the default.** `cacheMaxMemorySize: 0` turns off the built-in in-memory LRU, which is capped at 50 MB, and replaces it with an uncapped `Map`.
3. **Doesn't solve the problem the section describes.** The section motivates a custom handler with cache consistency across Kubernetes pods, but the `Map` is still per-process.
4. **Scales poorly on invalidation.** `revalidateTag` iterates over every entry.

The text says to "use this as a starting point and extend it with durable storage, eviction policies…", but the snippet looks complete and copy-pasteable. I have seen more than one production project ship it verbatim and then hit memory leaks.

### Is there any context that might help us understand?

Suggestions (any of these would help):

- Use a bounded store in the example, e.g. `lru-cache` with `maxSize` + `sizeCalculation`, or at least a size/TTL check in `set`.
- Put a visible warning (callout) directly above the snippet: "Not for production: this cache is unbounded and per-process."
- Alternatively, replace the in-memory snippet with a minimal external-store skeleton (the [Redis `cacheHandler` example](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/cache-handler-redis) is already linked) so the shown code actually achieves cross-instance sharing.

### Does the docs page already exist? Please link to it.

https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/self-hosting#configuring-caching

title: Scheduling badge counts change requests that aren't scheduled
body:
### How are you running Flagsmith
- [x] SaaS at flagsmith.com

### Describe the bug
The **Scheduling** item in the environment sidebar shows a count badge for change requests that were committed for immediate publish, not scheduled. The Scheduling page itself correctly shows no scheduled changes, and the badge clears on a page refresh.

### Steps To Reproduce
1. Enable change requests on an environment.
2. Load the dashboard and leave the tab open.
3. Create two change requests, approve and commit them, publishing immediately (no schedule).
4. Look at **Scheduling** in the environment sidebar — it shows a `2` badge.
5. Refresh the page — the badge disappears.

### Expected behavior
No badge, as there are no scheduled changes.

### Likely cause
`frontend/web/components/navigation/navbars/EnvironmentNavbar.tsx:24` pins `live_from_after` to the time the navbar mounted:

```ts
const date = useRef(moment().toISOString())
const { data: scheduledData } = useGetChangeRequestsQuery({
  committed: true, environmentId, live_from_after: date.current, page_size: 1,
})
```

A change request published immediately gets a `live_from` of its commit time, which is *after* that pinned timestamp, so the list endpoint returns it and the badge counts it as scheduled. Committing invalidates the `ChangeRequest` LIST tag, so the query refetches — but with the same stale timestamp. A refresh re-mounts the navbar with a current timestamp, so the change request drops out.

`frontend/web/components/pages/ScheduledChangesPage.tsx:40` pins the same value with `useMemo(..., [])`, so a long-lived session on that page will drift the same way.

Computing `live_from_after` at request time rather than at mount, or filtering server-side on "live in the future", would both fix it.

title: Bug: useId generating duplicate IDs
body:
Separate `useId()` calls can produce the same ID within a single server-rendered component tree, breaking ARIA references.

the reproduction seems to point to leading zeroes being lost when React serializes an overflowing tree-position ID.

React version: 19.3.1, the latest stable version checked. Also reproduced with 19.3.0, which the CodeSandbox currently pins. React and React DOM versions match in both cases.

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Open the CodeSandbox preview.
2. Observe the duplicate-ID report for both `renderToStaticMarkup` and `renderToReadableStream`.
3. Inspect the accessibility tree for “Card 23”. Its article is incorrectly named “Preview of card 1”.

The reproduction renders 32 cards inside 12 wrapper levels. Each card calls `useId()` for its heading, and its nested preview component independently calls `useId()` for its container.

Link to code example:
https://codesandbox.io/s/t28n3h?file=/repro.js

Live preview:
https://t28n3h.csb.app/

## The current behavior

Both renderers generate `_R_bqlala_` for:

- The first card’s preview.
- The 23rd card’s heading.

The 23rd article’s `aria-labelledby` consequently resolves to the first card’s preview instead of its own heading.

Changing the nesting depth or sibling count can avoid the collision.

## The expected behavior

Separate `useId()` calls within the same rendered tree should produce unique IDs, so each article’s `aria-labelledby` resolves to its own heading.

https://github.com/digasic/next-partial-prefetching-inline-action-hang

The app has `cacheComponents: true` and `partialPrefetching: true`; its only page renders (a) one `"use cache"` function, (b) a Server Component with an inline `"use server"` function that closes over a prop (`locale`), and (c) `cookies()` inside a Suspense boundary so the page is partially prerendered (`◐`).

title: Caught error from a 'use cache' function still fails the page (build error, 500) since 16.1.0
fix(Audit): Audit log search overloads the database
body:
## Problem

Audit log search (`GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/audit/?search=...`) can use all database CPU. A small number of requests on a project with a large audit log used all CPU on the primary database. The admin API and the SDK API both failed their health checks, and this caused a full outage.

## Cause

The `search` filter uses `icontains` on `AuditLog.log`. The ORM turns it into:

    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM audit_auditlog
    WHERE project_id = %s AND UPPER(log::text) LIKE UPPER('%term%')

1. The `%` at the start and `UPPER()` on the column block every index, so each request reads every audit log row of the project.
2. The pagination runs this scan two times: once for `COUNT(*)` and once for the page itself.
3. When the client or load balancer times out, the query keeps running in Postgres. Retries add more queries, so the load grows and connections are used up.

https://github.com/tamatebox/next-revalidate-clock-repro

### To Reproduce

1. `npm install && npm run build`
2. `CLOCK_AHEAD_MS=2000 NODE_OPTIONS="--require ./clock-ahead.cjs" npm start` — `clock-ahead.cjs` moves `Date.now()` 2 s ahead of `performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()`, as when the OS steps the wall clock forward after `next start` started
3. In another terminal, `npm run repro`: it warms `/` (ISR, `revalidate = 3600`), POSTs `/api/bump` (writes a new value and calls `revalidatePath("/")`), requests `/` right away, and again 2.5 s later

Without the preload (`npm start`), the request right after `revalidatePath("/")` is a `MISS` with the new value.

Current, with the wall clock 2 s ahead:

```
revalidatePath("/") after writing value=1793766976560
right after: value=1793766973376 x-nextjs-cache=HIT
2.5 s later: value=1793766976560 x-nextjs-cache=MISS

Expected: `revalidatePath` / `revalidateTag` expire the entry immediately, whatever the wall clock does.

The cause, as far as I can read it in `next@16.4.5` (same in 16.3.5):

- `dist/server/lib/incremental-cache/file-system-cache.js`, `revalidateTag`: `const now = Date.now();` → `tagsManifest.set(tag, { ...existingEntry, expired: now })`

When the wall clock runs ahead (an NTP step or slew forward, or after the machine sleeps — on macOS the monotonic clock does not advance during sleep), `expiredAt <= now` stays false for the size of the gap. title: Inconsistent listing of inherited abstract methods in collections.abc documentation
body:
### Documentation

Thanks for maintaining such comprehensive Python documentation!

While studying `collections.abc`, I noticed a small inconsistency in how inherited abstract methods are listed in the documentation table.

## Description

The "Abstract Methods" column does not consistently indicate whether it lists only methods declared directly in an ABC or all abstract methods that subclasses must implement.

For example:

- **`Reversible`** inherits from `Iterable`, so subclasses must implement both `__iter__()` and `__reversed__()`. However, the table lists only `__reversed__()`.
- **`Collection`** inherits from `Sized`, `Iterable`, and `Container`. The table lists all three inherited abstract methods: `__contains__()`, `__iter__()`, and `__len__()`.

This makes it difficult to determine the complete set of required methods from the table alone.

## Suggested improvement

I suggest distinguishing between directly declared abstract methods and all required abstract methods, including inherited ones.

For example:

| ABC | Inherits from | Directly declared abstract methods | All required abstract methods | Mixin methods |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Reversible` | `Iterable` | `__reversed__()` | `__iter__()`, `__reversed__()` | — |
| `Collection` | `Sized`, `Iterable`, `Container` | — | `__contains__()`, `__iter__()`, `__len__()` | — |

This structure clearly distinguishes abstract methods declared directly in each ABC from those inherited from parent classes, making the complete interface requirements easier to understand.

Alternatively, the existing table could simply list all required abstract methods consistently, without adding new columns.

Either approach would improve clarity and make the documentation easier to use when implementing custom classes.

This suggestion concerns documentation clarity only and does not require changes to Python's behavior.

I hope this suggestion is helpful. Thanks for your time and for considering it!

### Bug report

```python
import gc
import sys
import threading

stop = threading.Event()

def writer():
    while not stop.is_set():
        sys.stderr.write("x\n")

t = threading.Thread(target=writer)
t.start()

gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_COLLECTABLE)
for _ in range(1000):
    a = []
    a.append(a)
    del a
    gc.collect()
gc.set_debug(0)

stop.set()
t.join()
print("done")
```

From initial investigation, during a stop the world for GC debug collectables is printed which can occur whilst the `BufferedWriter` lock is being held. Debug for uncollectables is instead called outside this critical section and does not have this deadlock pattern.

title: `hashlib`: `usedforsecurity` works the wrong way round in FIPS mode in 3.14.10
body:
### Bug report

### Bug description:

In 3.14.10, when OpenSSL runs in FIPS mode, `usedforsecurity` does the opposite of what it should:

* `usedforsecurity=False`: MD5 should work, but OpenSSL refuses it.
* `usedforsecurity=True`: MD5 should be refused, but OpenSSL allows it.

Because `hashlib` can no longer get MD5 from OpenSSL, it quietly switches to its own built-in MD5 (`_md5`). The built-in MD5 does not check FIPS, so `hashlib.md5()` now works in FIPS mode with no error, even for security use.

3.14.9 and earlier work correctly.

#### Cause

The bug was introduced when the fix for gh-149816 was backported to 3.14 (GH-160006, commit 3d2f1b2d7aa). In `py_digest_by_name()` in `Modules/_hashopenssl.c`:

```c
int fips = disable_fips_property(py_ht);
if (fips == -1) {
    goto finally;
}
```

`disable_fips_property()` returns 1 for `usedforsecurity=False`. The code after it treats `fips == 1` as "use the strict FIPS lookup":

```c
PY_EVP_MD **cached = fips ? &entry->evp : &entry->evp_nosecurity;
...
fresh = PY_EVP_MD_fetch(entry->ossl_name, fips ? NULL : "-fips");
```

So the value needs to be inverted. `main` (GH-153019) and 3.15 (GH-159997) do this:

```c
int fips = !disable_fips_property(py_ht);
```

In 3.14 the backport kept a `-1` error return, and the `!` was lost when the code was adapted for it.

Affected: 3.14.10 and the current `3.14` branch.
Not affected (the source does not contain the bug): 3.14.9 and earlier, 3.13, 3.15, `main`.

#### How to reproduce

You need OpenSSL 3 in FIPS mode as described above, so that `_hashlib.get_fips_mode()` returns 1.

```python
import hashlib, _hashlib

print("fips mode:", _hashlib.get_fips_mode())

def t(label, f):
    try:
        f()
        print("ok    ", label)
    except Exception as e:
        print("ERROR ", label, "->", type(e).__name__, e)

t("openssl_md5(usedforsecurity=False)  [must work]",
  lambda: _hashlib.openssl_md5(b"x", usedforsecurity=False))
t("openssl_md5(usedforsecurity=True)   [must be refused]",

title: 16.4.5: Route Handlers drop `Content-Encoding` but still send the encoded body (breaks `hono/compress`, `CompressionStream`)
body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/maryayi/next-16-4-5-content-encoding-repro

### To Reproduce

The repo has two Route Handlers that return a gzip-encoded body with `Content-Encoding: gzip`:

- `app/api/[[...route]]/route.ts`: a Hono app using `hono/compress`, mounted with `handle` from `hono/vercel`
- `app/plain-gzip/route.ts`: no dependencies:

```ts
export async function GET() {
  const json = JSON.stringify({ hello: 'world' })
  const body = new Response(json).body!.pipeThrough(new CompressionStream('gzip'))
  return new Response(body, {
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', 'content-encoding': 'gzip' },
  })
}
```

Then:

```bash
npm install
bash compare.sh 16.4.4
bash compare.sh 16.4.5
bash compare.sh canary
```

`compare.sh` installs the given version, runs `next build` + `next start`, prints the response headers and the first body bytes, then runs `fetch(url).then(r => r.json())` like a browser would.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

With `next@16.4.4`, both routes:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-encoding: gzip
content-type: application/json
first body bytes:  1f 8b 08 00
response.json(): OK
```

With `next@16.4.5` and `next@16.5.0-canary.41`, both routes:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json
first body bytes:  1f 8b 08 00
response.json(): SyntaxError: Unexpected token '\x1f', "\x1f\xfffd\x08\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x03"... is not valid JSON
```

The `Content-Encoding` header is removed, but the body is still gzip. The client has no way to know it must decode it, so it gets raw gzip bytes. `next dev` behaves the same way.

**Expected:** when a Route Handler returns a body it encoded itself and sets `Content-Encoding` to match, the header is kept, as in 16.4.4.

### Provide environment information

```bash
Operating System:
  Platform: linux
  Arch: x64

title: Audit hooks added before `Py_Initialize()` are freed with the wrong allocator, crashing at exit
body:
### Crash report

I've been looking into the performance of streaming decompression with `compression.zstd`, first on 3.14 and 3.15, then on the free-threaded builds. That turned up a memory issue in free-threaded builds, which I'm reporting separately. This crash is something I ran into along the way.

While reproducing the memory issue on a Windows machine, the runs with `PYTHONMALLOC=mimalloc` on 3.15 crashed at exit with an access violation, after the script itself had finished fine. Even `python -c pass` crashed. 3.14 didn't, and neither did any run without `PYTHONMALLOC`.

It turned out the machine's endpoint security agent loads into `python.exe` and registers an audit hook with `PySys_AddAuditHook()` before `Py_Initialize()`. That's allowed: the [docs](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/sys.html#c.PySys_AddAuditHook) say the function "is safe to call before `Py_Initialize`". But the hook's list entry is allocated with `PyMem_RawMalloc()` at that point, before `PYTHONMALLOC` is applied, so it comes from `malloc()`. At finalization, `_PySys_ClearAuditHooks()` frees it with `PyMem_RawFree()`, which by then is mimalloc's. `mi_free()` on a block from the C heap crashes.

Anything that changes the raw allocator at startup has the same problem:
- `PYTHONMALLOC=mimalloc` on builds with the GIL, since 3.15 (before, it left the raw domain on `malloc()`);
- the debug hooks, since 3.13 at least: `-X dev` / `PYTHONDEVMODE=1` and the `*_debug` allocators. There the crash is sometimes caught as

  ```
  Fatal Python error: _PyMem_DebugRawFree: bad ID: Allocated using API '', verified using API 'r'
  ```

I think #161074 is this bug: a crash in audit-hook cleanup under `-X dev` on Windows, on a machine with a security product installed, closed without a root cause.

### Reproducer

You don't need an agent for this. CPython's own embedding test program adds a hook before `Py_Initialize()`, and in a source build it crashes the same way:

```console
$ PYTHONMALLOC=mimalloc ./Prog

title: Free-threaded 3.14.10 and 3.15.2 keep memory freed by other threads: 10 GB peaks since the mimalloc 2.5.2 update
body:
### Bug report

I've been looking into the performance of streaming decompression with `compression.zstd` (archive extraction in a package manager), first on 3.14 and 3.15, then on the free-threaded builds. On 3.14.10t, extracting an archive with 1.1 GiB of files peaked at 1.3 GB, against 170 MB on 3.14.

The extraction decompresses on worker threads and hands the decompressed `bytes` to one thread that writes them out. Boiled down: worker threads make large `bytes` objects, the main thread consumes and drops them, with a bounded number in flight. That needs about 150 MiB at any time, but on 3.14.10t, 3.15.2t and current `main` the peak grows to 9–10 GB:

```python
import resource
import sys
from collections import deque
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

BLOCK, COUNT, THREADS = 16 << 20, 1536, 8      # 24 GiB in total
pattern = bytes(range(256)) * (BLOCK // 256)

def produce(i):
    return memoryview(pattern).tobytes()         # a new bytes object, as decompress() returns

with ThreadPoolExecutor(THREADS) as pool:
    pending = deque()
    for i in range(COUNT):
        pending.append(pool.submit(produce, i))
        if len(pending) >= THREADS:
            pending.popleft().result()           # freed here, on the main thread
    for future in pending:
        future.result()

peak = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
peak = peak if sys.platform == "darwin" else peak * 1024
print(f"{sys.version.split()[0]}{'' if sys._is_gil_enabled() else 't'}: peak RSS {peak >> 20} MiB")
```

macOS 26 (arm64), python-build-standalone builds, and `main` built from source:

| Python | vendored mimalloc | peak RSS |
|---|---|---:|
| 3.14.10 (default allocator) | — | 167 MiB |
| 3.13.18t | 2.1.2 | 392 MiB |
| 3.14.10t | 2.5.2 | **9,933 MiB** |
| 3.15.2t | 2.5.2 | **10,266 MiB** |
| 3.15.2, `PYTHONMALLOC=mimalloc` | 2.5.2 | **10,453 MiB** |
| 3.16.0a1t, tagged before the update | 2.1.2 | 430 MiB |
| `main` (aaaf61c), free-threaded | 2.5.2 | **8,994 MiB**

title: tkinter with pre-release versions of Tk 9.0.5 or 8.6.18 drops all events sent to widgets in a hidden window
body:
### Bug report

With the python.org macOS installer for **3.13.17**, widgets inside a hidden toplevel (withdrawn, or iconified) receive no events. This includes events sent synchronously with `event_generate` and ttk's `<<ThemeChanged>>`. The events are dropped rather than deferred: none are delivered after the window is shown. **3.13.16** with the same Tk patchlevel (8.6.18) delivers them all, as do Windows and Linux builds.

```python
import sys
import tkinter as tk
from tkinter import ttk

root = tk.Tk()
print("python", sys.version.split()[0], "tk", root.tk.call("info", "patchlevel"))


def run(label, hide):
    top = tk.Toplevel(root)
    hide(top)
    frame = ttk.Frame(top, width=50, height=50)
    hits = []
    for ev in ("<Enter>", "<<Custom>>", "<<ThemeChanged>>"):
        frame.bind(ev, lambda e, ev=ev: hits.append(ev), "+")
    frame.pack()
    root.update()
    frame.event_generate("<Enter>")
    frame.event_generate("<<Custom>>")
    style = ttk.Style()
    style.theme_use("alt" if style.theme_use() != "alt" else "clam")
    root.update()
    hidden = list(hits)
    top.deiconify()
    root.update()
    print(f"{label:24} while hidden: {hidden}  after show: {hits[len(hidden):]}")
    top.destroy()


def shown_then_withdrawn(top):
    root.update()
    top.withdraw()
    root.update()


run("never shown, withdrawn", lambda t: t.withdraw())
run("shown, then withdrawn", shown_then_withdrawn)
run("iconified", lambda t: t.iconify())
root.destroy()
```

title: Show which tuple item is unhashable when a nested dict key or set element is rejected
body:
### Feature or enhancement

`{([1],): 1}` looks contrived, but this comes up in real code as soon as a tuple
key is built from existing data:

```python
row = {"user": "alice", "tags": ["a", "b"]}
groups = {}
groups.setdefault((row["user"], row["tags"]), [])
```

```
TypeError: cannot use 'tuple' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'list')
```

Tuples are normally valid keys, so the message appears to reject the tuple because
of a list that isn't visibly related to it. Nothing says that the list is inside
the tuple, or where. This was pointed out on gh-132825 and again in the PEP 814
thread, and it is harder to follow with deeper nesting or longer tuples.

I'd suggest adding a note in the error path of `tuple_hash`, following what the
`json` module already does for nested values:

```pycon
>>> json.dumps({"a": [1, object()]})
TypeError: Object of type object is not JSON serializable
when serializing list item 1
when serializing dict item 'a'

>>> hash(("alice", ["a", "b"]))  # proposed
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
when hashing tuple item 1
```

The note would be added only after an item's hash has failed, so successful hashing
is unaffected. Nested tuples would produce one note per level.

**Dependency on gh-149313:** the dict and set paths currently replace the exception
and discard its notes, so the note would only become visible for dict keys and set
elements once that issue is fixed. Until then, only direct `hash()` calls would
show it.

Reproduced on 3.14.6 and 3.15.0b2.

I noticed this behavior and found it confusing myself, and the proposal is my own. I used Claude to help write this up in English and to re-check the behavior.

### Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

This is a minor feature, which does not need previous discussion elsewhere

title: `python -m random N` prints a float for an integer N <= 0
body:
### Bug report

### Bug description:

The command-line interface of `random` documents that, when no option is given, an integer input is handled "same as `--integer`". For an integer that is zero or negative, it prints a random float instead:

```shell
$ python -m random -i 0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: empty range in randint(1, 0)
$ python -m random 0
0.0
$ python -m random -5
-2.8133945085995364
```

`main()` calls `randint()` inside the same `try` block that converts the input with `int()`:

```python
try:
    # Is it an integer?
    val = int(val)
    return randint(1, val)
except ValueError:
    try:
        # Is it a float?
        val = float(val)
        return uniform(0, val)
```

so the `ValueError` that `randint()` raises for an empty range is taken to mean that the input is not an integer, and the input is then handled as a float. Keeping only the `int()` call inside the `try` block makes `python -m random N` behave like `python -m random --integer N` for every integer.

title: The hot attribute is not enabled when building CPython with Clang's default configuration
body:
### Bug report

Build CPython with Clang's default configuration.
```bash
./configure CC=clang LDFLAGS='-fuse-ld=lld'
make -j
```
Although `_PyEval_EvalFrameDefault` in `Python/ceval.c` is marked with `_Py_HOT_FUNCTION`, the output of `readelf -SW Python/ceval.o` does not contain `.text.hot.` section. 

This is because CPython uses `__GNUC__` and `__GNUC_MINOR__`  to determine whether the hot attribute is supported.
```c
#if defined(__GNUC__) \
    && ((__GNUC__ >= 5) || (__GNUC__ == 4) && (__GNUC_MINOR__ >= 3))
#define _Py_HOT_FUNCTION __attribute__((hot))
#else
#define _Py_HOT_FUNCTION
#endif
```

In Clang, the default values for these macros are as follows.
```
__GNUC__=4
__GNUC_MINOR__=2
__GNUC_PATCHLEVEL__=1
```

Therefore, I propose to use `_Py__has_attribute(hot)` or `GCC version >= 4.3` to determine whether this attribute is supported as follows.
```c
#if _Py__has_attribute(hot) || defined(__GNUC__) \
    && ((__GNUC__ >= 5) || (__GNUC__ == 4) && (__GNUC_MINOR__ >= 3))
#define _Py_HOT_FUNCTION __attribute__((hot))
#else
#define _Py_HOT_FUNCTION
#endif
```

The history of compiler support for the relevant features is as follows.
* GCC introduced `__attribute__((hot))` in GCC 4.3.0.
  * https://gcc.gnu.org/pipermail/gcc-patches/2017-July/478580.html
* GCC has supported for `__has_attribute()` since GCC 5.
  * https://gcc.gnu.org/gcc-5/changes.html
* Clang has supported `__attribute__((hot))` since Clang 3.2.
  * https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/commit/29c2b4330ce07a7af7452cf3ad2528d0e31952b0
* Clang has supported `__has_attribute()` since Clang 2.9.
  * https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/commit/274a70ed7f4315c83273173fce4c3b0e097958d6
* By default, Clang defines `__GNUC__` as 4, `__GNUC_MINOR__` as 2, and `__GNUC_PATCHLEVEL__` as 1.
  * https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/99804

title: ctypes: structures with float arrays returned by value are wrong on Linux SPARC
body:
### Bug report

test_ctypes fails on Linux sparc64 in test_array_in_struct: a structure with a small array of doubles returned by value comes back as garbage. 8 and 9 doubles are fine, those are returned in memory.

On Linux, GCC and clang pass arrays of floating-point type inside a structure in integer registers. Only Solaris follows the vendor ABI there, GCC changed that for Solaris only: https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=114416. Since gh-110190 ctypes describes the array elements to libffi as floats on all SPARC, so on Linux libffi reads the result from the FP registers.

Describing the elements as integers of the same size on Linux fixes it, Solaris stays as it is. Long double arrays have the same problem, I'll send that separately with a test.

When one task awaits another through a Future, `python -m asyncio pstree` omits the awaited task from the tree

Repro:

    asyncio.current_task().set_name("main")

    future = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()

title: zoneinfo: ZoneInfo() raises OSError instead of ZoneInfoNotFoundError for an overlong key when tzdata is installed
body:
# Bug report

### Bug description:

When the `tzdata` package is installed, `zoneinfo.ZoneInfo` with a key longer than the file name limit raises `OSError` (`ENAMETOOLONG`) instead of `ZoneInfoNotFoundError`:

```python
import zoneinfo
zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("9" * 300)
```

Without `tzdata`:

```
zoneinfo._common.ZoneInfoNotFoundError: 'No time zone found with key 999…'
```

With `tzdata` installed (`pip install tzdata`):

```
OSError: [Errno 36] File name too long: '…/site-packages/tzdata/zoneinfo/999…'
```

The lookup in the system time zone path ends up with `os.path.isfile()`, which returns `False` for such a name. The fallback in `zoneinfo._common.load_tzdata()` then opens the resource, and its `except` clause only converts `ImportError`, `FileNotFoundError`, `UnicodeEncodeError` and `IsADirectoryError` into `ZoneInfoNotFoundError`. `ENAMETOOLONG` (and likely other `OSError`s from an invalid name) escapes.

Code that validates untrusted time zone names with `except ZoneInfoNotFoundError` therefore gets an unexpected exception. Found through the test suite of probatio, which feeds hostile input to its time zone validator. This came up while packaging Home Assistant 2026.11 for Yocto/OpenEmbedded: https://github.com/meta-homeassistant/meta-homeassistant/pull/207

title: `curses.tparm()` crashes for capabilities that take string parameters
body:
### Bug description:

`curses.tparm()` passes all its parameters as integers. But ncurses treats some parameters as `char *`, for the few capabilities that take strings: `pfkey`, `pfloc`, `pfx`, `pln`, `pfxl`, and the extended `Cs` and `Ms` of xterm. So passing an integer there crashes:

```python
import curses
curses.setupterm('xterm-256color')
curses.tparm(curses.tigetstr('Ms'), 1)    # Segmentation fault
```

The same happens with `curses.tigetstr('Cs')`. There is also no way to pass a string, so these capabilities cannot be used from Python at all.

ncurses takes as strings the parameters for which `%s` or `%l` directly follows `%p`N, but only in the format strings of the capabilities above of the current terminal. For other format strings with such parameters it returns `NULL`, so a plain `b'%p1%s'` does not crash: `tparm()` raises `curses.error`.

NetBSD curses takes such parameters as strings in any format string, not only in those capabilities, so with it even `curses.tparm(b'x%p1%sy', 1)` crashes.

title: Backport gh-144248 to 3.14: pyrepl on Windows loops forever printing tracebacks when stdin is the NUL device
body:
# Bug report

### Bug description:

On Windows with Python 3.14.x, starting the REPL with the `NUL` device as stdin and a pipe as stdout makes `_pyrepl` print the same traceback in an endless loop. The output never stops. In one real incident, an unattended process wrote **5.38 GB** of identical tracebacks to a log file over about 26 minutes before it was killed.

This is easy to trigger by accident. In Git Bash (MSYS), both an empty heredoc and `</dev/null` give the child process the Windows `NUL` device as stdin, and `os.isatty()` returns `True` for it. So the `isatty` check in `_pyrepl/main.py` passes and pyrepl is chosen.

**Reproduction** (Git Bash on Windows 11, python.org 3.14.3):

```bash
$ timeout 3 python - <<'EOF' 2>&1 | wc -c
EOF
14266063
```

That is about 14 MB in 3 seconds. Every iteration prints:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "...\Lib\_pyrepl\readline.py", line 395, in multiline_input
    return reader.readline()
  File "...\Lib\_pyrepl\reader.py", line 752, in readline
    self.prepare()
  File "...\Lib\_pyrepl\historical_reader.py", line 306, in prepare
    super().prepare()
  File "...\Lib\_pyrepl\reader.py", line 585, in prepare
    self.console.prepare()
  File "...\Lib\_pyrepl\windows_console.py", line 359, in prepare
    self.height, self.width = self.getheightwidth()
  File "...\Lib\_pyrepl\windows_console.py", line 410, in getheightwidth
    raise WinError(GetLastError())
OSError: [WinError 123] <localized: The filename, directory name, or volume label syntax is incorrect.>
```

The error code is stale. That matches gh-132888, where `ctypes.GetLastError()` was used incorrectly. Because the console error is not caught at init time, pyrepl gets as far as the interactive loop. There, the bare `except:` in `run_multiline_interactive_console` (`simple_interact.py`) shows the traceback and retries, so the persistent error turns into an infinite loop.

- `printf '' | python -` exits 0 w

title: dict.setdefault() segfaults on an instance dict with an absent shared key passed as a str subclass
body:
### Crash report

`setdefault()` crashes when a str-subclass key equals a shared key that has no value in this instance's `__dict__`. No callbacks, threads or C extension are needed. An exact `str` key takes a different, safe path.

```python
class C:
    pass
a = C()
a.x = 1
b = C()
b.y = 2
d = b.__dict__
class S(str):
    pass
print('get', d.get(S('x'), 'default'), flush=True)
print('setdefault', d.setdefault(S('x'), 5), flush=True)
```

Recorded on 3.15.2 and main: prints `get default`, then SIGSEGV in `setdefault()`. Expected: return `5` and insert the missing key. The record also reproduces the crash with a `StrEnum` member in place of the str subclass.

Cause: Objects/dictobject.c:4817-4841 uses the split-table insertion path only for exact str keys. The generic `_Py_dict_lookup` can return a nonnegative index with `value == NULL` when the shared key exists but this instance has no value. The test at :4843 checks only `ix == DKIX_EMPTY`; :4865-4869 then reaches `Py_NewRef(value)` with NULL. The missing-value test needs `|| value == NULL`, as other lookup callers in this file already use.

title: Thread.join(timeout) can block forever: ThreadHandle_join reads the clock twice through Py_MAX (3.13, 3.14)
body:
**Bug report**

`ThreadHandle_join` in `Modules/_threadmodule.c` recomputes the time left of a timed join as

```c
// _PyDeadline_Get will return a negative value if the deadline has
// been exceeded.
timeout_ns = Py_MAX(_PyDeadline_Get(deadline), 0);
```

(3.13 branch, line 517; 3.14 branch, line 544; also in v3.13.16 and v3.14.0.)

`Py_MAX(x, y)` is `(((x) > (y)) ? (x) : (y))` (`Include/pymacro.h`), so it evaluates `_PyDeadline_Get(deadline)` twice. The first read is compared with 0 and the second is the one returned. If the deadline passes between the two reads, the first is positive, the second is negative, and a negative `timeout_ns` is returned. The loop then calls `PyEvent_WaitTimed(..., timeout_ns, ...)` with it, and `_PySemaphore_PlatformWait` in `Python/parking_lot.c` treats `timeout < 0` as "no timeout" (`INFINITE` on Windows; the untimed `sem_wait`/`pthread_cond_wait` branch on POSIX). The `if (timeout_ns)` check after it does not catch a negative value. `Thread.join(timeout)` then never returns.

`_PyMutex_LockTimed` in `Python/lock.c` clamps correctly ("Avoid negative values because those mean block forever"), so only the timed `Thread.join` is exposed.

**Why it needs a wait that ends early.** The window is the interval between the two clock reads, after a wait that ended a little before the deadline. On Windows, wait timeouts are counted in timer ticks (15.6 ms by default) while the deadline uses the high-resolution clock, so a wait often ends a fraction of a tick early and sends the loop around again. A program that joins in a loop with a short timeout gives it many chances.

**Observed.** A pyqtgraph window's GUI thread (Windows 11, Python 3.13.16 from conda-forge) polled `worker.join(0.02)` fifty times a second. It hung repeatedly, within 0.5 to 5.5 hours of starting. Caught live, the hung process's main thread used no CPU in ten seconds, its Python stack was in `Thread.join`, and its native stack, read with dbghelp and the matching `python313.pdb

title: Windows: update zlib-ng to 2.2.5 (PGO builds with Visual Studio 17.11 decompress wrongly on AVX-512 CPUs)
body:
### Bug report

On Windows, a PGO build made with Visual Studio 17.11 (MSVC 14.41, `MSC v.1941`) decompresses deflate data wrongly on CPUs with AVX-512 (here a Ryzen 9 7950X): `test_zlib` (`test_decompressmaxlen*`: "incorrect data check"), `test_gzip` (`test_write_seek_write`: "CRC check failed") and `test_tarfile` fail. The checks are right, the data is wrong: raw inflate of an intact file returns different bytes than Linux `gzip`, and `zlib.crc32()` is correct. Builds without PGO and the python.org builds (newer compiler) are fine.

This is https://github.com/zlib-ng/zlib-ng/issues/1883: MSVC from Visual Studio 17.11 miscompiles `GET_CHUNK_MAG()` (`arch/x86/chunkset_avx512.c`, used for back-references shorter than 32 bytes). zlib-ng 2.2.5 works around it (https://github.com/zlib-ng/zlib-ng/pull/1884) by turning optimization off for that function for Visual Studio before 17.13 (`_MSC_VER < 1943`). main, 3.15 and 3.14 bundle 2.2.4.

As discussed on [#131438](https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/131438#issuecomment-6745946589), I would like to request updating the Windows build to zlib-ng 2.2.5. 2.2.5 also checks for ZMM support before using the VPCLMULQDQ CRC code that CPython builds (https://github.com/zlib-ng/zlib-ng/pull/1932) and reverts a `deflate_medium` change that regressed performance (https://github.com/zlib-ng/zlib-ng/pull/1938). I'm happy to test a build on the affected machine.

- Sources: https://github.com/zlib-ng/zlib-ng/archive/refs/tags/2.2.5.tar.gz, SHA-256 `5b3b022489f3ced82384f06db1e13ba148cbce38c7941e424d6cb414416acd18` (downloaded 2026-11-09)

title: Use the Neri–Schneider algorithm for ordinal-to-date conversion in datetime
body:
### Proposal

`ord_to_ymd()` in `Modules/_datetimemodule.c` and `_ord2ymd()` in `Lib/_pydatetime.py`
convert a proleptic Gregorian ordinal to (year, month, day). They still use the
algorithm from 2002: four divisions by the 400/100/4/1-year cycle lengths, a
special case for December 31 at the end of a 4- or 400-year cycle, and a month
estimate that is "either exact or one too large" and is corrected afterwards
(for about 24% of dates).

Neri and Schneider, "Euclidean affine functions and their application to
calendar algorithms" (Softw Pract Exper. 2023;53(4):937–970,
https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.06959) give an algorithm with no lookup tables and
no estimate-and-correct step. GCC's libstdc++, the Linux kernel, .NET and Go
already use it. I propose replacing both functions with their Figure 12.

The conversion is used by `date.fromordinal()`, `date.fromisocalendar()`,
`fromisoformat()` with ISO week dates, `strptime()` with `%j` or week
directives, and `date`/`datetime` ± `timedelta` when the result leaves the
current month by more than one day.

### Verification

- Same results as `main` for all 3,652,059 ordinals (0001-01-01 … 9999-12-31):
  SHA-256 over every `date.fromordinal()` result, plus `fromisocalendar()` and
  `date + timedelta`, for both the C and the pure-Python implementations.
- C: same results for every positive `int` ordinal (1 … 2**31-1), including
  the error messages past 9999-12-31; checked with gcc 13 and clang.
- Pure Python: same results for 2.3 million other integers, including negative
  and huge ones.
- test_datetime, test_calendar, test_strptime, test_time, test_zoneinfo,
  test_plistlib and test_xmlrpc pass. The PR adds a test for the first and
  last days of every month in years at the ends of the 4-, 100- and 400-year
  cycles.

### Benchmarks

pyperf, x86-64 VM, gcc 13.3, `-O3`, no PGO; µs per 1000 operations:

| Benchmark | main | patched | Speedup |

| `date.fromordinal`, random dates | 35.6 | 25.3 | 1.40x |

title: Free-threaded GC can abort during concurrent subinterpreter teardown
body:
### Crash report

[OpTree](https://github.com/metaopt/optree/) CI hit this assertion on an unmodified Windows x64 free-threaded debug build of CPython 3.14.10 (`b703b2c`). An `InterpreterPoolExecutor` worker was destroying its interpreter. The native stack went from `Py_EndInterpreter()` through shutdown GC to `mi_abandoned_visit_blocks()` and `validate_alive_bits()`.

CI backtrace: https://github.com/metaopt/optree/actions/runs/42811376193/job/129813367183#step:18:1

```text
Python/gc_free_threading.c:1082: validate_alive_bits:
Assertion "!gc_is_alive(op)" failed: object should not be marked as alive yet
```

I suspect a race in the abandoned-segment scan introduced with the mimalloc 2.5.2 update. One interpreter can temporarily clear a segment’s bitmap bit, discover that the segment belongs to another interpreter, and restore the bit. The owning interpreter’s GC reads the bitmap **before** acquiring `abandoned_visit_lock`. If it reads during that interval, it can skip the segment. The same scan is present on `main` at `9d4a35c`.

Allocator code: https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.14.10/Objects/mimalloc/arena-abandon.c#L209-L269

- 3.14 backport: #160183

---

### Standard Library Reproducer

Starting from `v3.14.10`, add `usleep(100);` inside the foreign-segment branch of `mi_arena_segment_clear_abandoned_at()`, immediately before it restores the bitmap bit.

```diff
   if (segment->subproc != subproc) {
+    usleep(100);
     // it is from another sub-process, re-mark it and continue searching
```

Build with `./configure --with-pydebug --disable-gil` and `make`. Save this as `repro.py` and run `./python.exe -I -X dev repro.py` on macOS.

```python
from concurrent import interpreters
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from threading import Barrier

workers = 8
barrier = Barrier(workers)


def run(_worker_id):
    for _ in range(10):
        interp = interpreters.create()
        barrier.wait()
        interp.exec('import gc\ngc.collect()')

title: ssl docs: custom client socket example never connects
body:
The [custom-context client example](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ssl.html#socket-creation) wraps a new socket and immediately prints `ssock.version()`. It never calls `connect()`, so `version()` returns `None` and no TLS connection is made.

The [`SSLContext.wrap_socket()` description](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ssl.html#ssl.SSLContext.wrap_socket) also says that "context construction" is deferred for an unconnected client socket. The context already exists; CPython creates the underlying SSL object when `SSLSocket.connect()` is called. The example should connect before printing the negotiated version, and the description should name the deferred operation.

title: Support path-like objects in shutil.which()
body:
`shutil.which()` accepts a `bytes` command and returns a `bytes` path. It also accepts path-like command objects, but a path-like object whose `__fspath__()` method returns `bytes` raises `TypeError` instead of behaving like the equivalent direct `bytes` value.

```python
import shutil


class BytesPath:
    def __fspath__(self):
        return b"python3"


print(shutil.which(b"python3"))
print(shutil.which(BytesPath()))
```

On CPython main, the first call returns a bytes path and the second fails:

```text
b'/usr/bin/python3'
TypeError: Can't mix strings and bytes in path components
```

`which()` checks whether `cmd` is `bytes` before resolving the path-like object. It then decodes `PATH` to `str`, while `os.path.split()` has resolved the command to `bytes`. Calling `os.fspath(cmd)` before choosing the string or bytes path keeps the command and search path on the same type.

### CPython versions tested on

- CPython main branch (`3.16.0a2+`)

title: Crash when a callable iterator is shared between threads
body:
### Crash report

### What happened?

In the free-threaded build, an `iter(callable, sentinel)` iterator that is used from several threads can crash the interpreter.

`calliter_iternext()` calls `it_callable` and compares the result against `it_sentinel` through borrowed pointers. Another thread can concurrently clear those fields when the iterator is exhausted, or replace `it_sentinel` / `it_stop_exc` in `__setstate__()`, freeing an object that is still in use. Two threads that exhaust the iterator at the same time can also both `Py_DECREF` the same callable and sentinel.

Reproducer (segfaults within a few seconds on a free-threaded release build of main):

```python
import threading

N = 2000

def worker(its, barrier):
    barrier.wait()
    for it in its:
        for _ in it:
            pass

for _ in range(200):
    # Each iterator holds the only reference to its callable.
    its = [iter(lambda: None, None) for _ in range(N)]
    barrier = threading.Barrier(4)
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(its, barrier))
               for _ in range(4)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
```

The default (GIL) build is not affected.

title: ElementTree: invalid paths raise KeyError instead of SyntaxError, and C and Python disagree on them
body:
### Bug report

### Bug description

Some malformed paths make `find()`, `findall()` and `findtext()` raise a bare `KeyError` from `ElementPath`, while other malformed paths raise `SyntaxError("invalid path")`. Which paths reach that code also depends on the implementation:

```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

root = ET.Element("root")
root.find("@")     # KeyError: '@'   (C accelerator and pure Python)
root.find("x=y")   # pure Python: KeyError: '='   C accelerator: None
root.find(")")     # pure Python: KeyError: ')'   C accelerator: None
root.find("]")     # pure Python: KeyError: ']'   C accelerator: None
```

(The pure-Python results can be reproduced by blocking the accelerator: `sys.modules["_elementtree"] = None` before importing `xml.etree.ElementTree`.)

**Cause.** `ElementPath.iterfind()` looks up each token with `ops[token[0]]`. Tokens that start no supported step (`@`, `=`, `(`, `)`, `]`, `!=`, `::`) are not in `ops`, so the lookup raises `KeyError`. The C accelerator only hands a path to `ElementPath` when its `checkpath()` finds one of `/ * [ @ .`; any other path is compared to tags literally. So `x=y`, `)` and `]` never reach the lookup in C, but always do in the pure-Python implementation.

**Expected.** `SyntaxError("invalid path")` for every path `ElementPath` cannot parse, as it already raises for other malformed paths. For example, replace the lookup with `ops.get(token[0])` and raise `SyntaxError` when it is missing.

Whether the C fast path should also send such paths to `ElementPath`, so that both implementations agree, is a separate choice. It would change results for existing code that looks up literal tags such as `"a b"` or `"a:b"`, so I am only proposing the `SyntaxError` change.

 I'm happy to open a PR.

title: `_PyEval_EvalFrameDefault` not in the call stack when interpreter is built with `--with-tail-call-interp`
body:
Found in numpy in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/33290

Numpy uses a "hack" to do temporary elision for arithmetic expressions to avoid allocating memory for temporaries. One thing it does to enable this elision is to detect "Am I being called directly by the python interpreter?" and part of that check is the question, "Is `_PyEval_EvalFrameDefault` in the call stack?".
Now on my macos machine for example with clang, If I'm on an interpreter that was built with `--with-tail-call-interp` such as the conda-forge build of cpython, `_PyEval_EvalFrameDefault` is no longer in the call stack and temporary elision is disabled so users lose this nice performance boost. On that issue I was informed that `_PyEval_EvalFrameDefault` should still be in the call stack and in turns out that this is probably PGO inlining as marking `_PyEval_EvalFrameDefault` with `Py_NO_INLINE` brings it back in the call stack. Is there any chance cpython can do something about that? Such as making the function Py_NO_INLINE? I'd be happy to send a patch if that's a fine approach.

Here are some call stacks with lldb to showcase my point that I got with `spin lldb -- $(pyenv which python) -P -c 'import numpy as np; n = 1<<16; np.ones(n) + np.ones(n) + np.ones(n)'`

Without tail-call interpeter:

title: ctypes: array slice assignment replaces the value's `__len__` exception with a ValueError
body:
### Bug report

## Summary

Assigning a sequence to a slice of a ctypes array calls `PySequence_Length` on the value. When the value's `__len__` raises, `PySequence_Length` returns `-1` with the exception set, and the code reads the `-1` as a length. The comparison `-1 != slicelen` is always true, so it raises its own `ValueError("Can only assign sequence of same size")` over the pending exception, which replaces it.

Expected: the exception from `__len__` should propagate.

## Reproducer

```python
import ctypes

class BadLen:
    def __len__(self):
        raise KeyError("len raised")

arr = (ctypes.c_int * 3)()
arr[0:1] = BadLen()
```

```console
ValueError: Can only assign sequence of same size
```

title: Fold PUSH_NULL; LOAD_CONST None into GET_AWAITABLE and GET_ANEXT
body:
### Feature or enhancement

Since gh-145667, `SEND` takes `(receiver, null_or_index, value)`. As a result, every `await` and every
`async for` iteration compiles to:

```
GET_AWAITABLE / GET_ANEXT
PUSH_NULL
LOAD_COMMON_CONSTANT     7 (None)
SEND
```

Both opcodes are only ever emitted immediately before this pair. I propose that they push the NULL and
the `None` themselves:

* `GET_AWAITABLE`: `(iterable -- iter, null, none)`
* `GET_ANEXT`: `(aiter -- aiter, awaitable, null, none)`

This saves two dispatches per `await` and per `async for` step. Opnames and opargs are unchanged and
`SEND` is untouched, so this is only a stack-effect change, like the one `GET_ITER` got in gh-132554.

No response given

title: zipfile honors inconsistent compression method state when extracting
body:
### Bug report

Moving from GHSA to public after discussion consensus.

## Summary

An user can contrive a ZIP input such that Python's zipfile attempts to decompress a member of the file with a different decompression method than other parsers will select. This can result in an extraction differential.

## Details

ZIP entries record their compression method in two places: the local header and the central directory.

Python honors the central directory entry's compression method, even if it differs from the local file entry's stated method. Consequently, Python will attempt to decompress an entry with an inconsistent method.

The correct behavior is to reject the discrepancy, similarly to how Python already rejects file name discrepancies between the local header and central directory.

## PoC

```python
import binascii
import io
import struct
import zipfile

original = b"central-directory interpretation\n" * 4

# Produce a valid DEFLATED archive and close it so the central directory exists.
buf = io.BytesIO()
with zipfile.ZipFile(buf, "w", compression=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:
    z.writestr("test.txt", original)

raw = bytearray(buf.getvalue())

with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(raw), "r") as z:
    info = z.getinfo("test.txt")

local = info.header_offset
assert raw[local : local + 4] == b"PK\x03\x04"

name_len, extra_len = struct.unpack_from("<HH", raw, local + 26)
data_start = local + 30 + name_len + extra_len
compressed = bytes(raw[data_start : data_start + info.compress_size])

# Rewrite ONLY the local header to describe a valid STORED member.
#
# Local-header offsets:
#   +8:  compression method (uint16)
#   +14: CRC-32             (uint32)
#   +18: compressed size    (uint32)
#   +22: uncompressed size  (uint32)
struct.pack_into("<H", raw, local + 8, zipfile.ZIP_STORED)
struct.pack_into(
    "<III",
    raw,
    local + 14,
    binascii.crc32(compressed) & 0xFFFFFFFF,
    len(compressed),
    len(compressed),
)

central = raw.index(b"PK\x01\x02")
local_meth

title: `x *= seq` raises TypeError for int subclasses and IntEnum where `x * seq` works
body:
### Bug report

When the left operand is an instance of a Python class that supports `__index__` but has no `__mul__`/`__imul__` that handles sequences (an `int` subclass, an `IntEnum` member, or any class with `__index__`), `x *= [1]` raises `TypeError`, while `x * [1]` and `x = x * [1]` work. With a plain `int` on the left it works.

```python
import enum, operator

class MyInt(int):
    pass

class Number(enum.IntEnum):
    TWO = 2

x = MyInt(2)
print(x * [1])              # [1, 1]
x *= [1]                    # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for *=: 'MyInt' and 'list'

y = Number.TWO
y *= [1]                    # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for *=: 'Number' and 'list'

operator.imul(MyInt(2), [1])  # same TypeError
```

Expected: `[1, 1]` in each case, the same as `x * [1]`.

The cause is in `PyNumber_InPlaceMultiply` (Objects/abstract.c): the right operand's `sq_repeat` is only tried in an `else if (mw != NULL)` branch, which is skipped whenever the left operand's type has a `tp_as_sequence` at all, even if that has no repeat slot. Every heap type has `tp_as_sequence`, so for these classes the list's repeat is never reached. `PyNumber_Multiply` does not have this problem because it checks the right operand independently.

### CPython versions tested on:

3.15, CPython main branch

### Operating systems tested on:

Linux

---
Found while building a Lean 4 model of CPython (https://broyojo.com/python-formalization/). AI tools (Claude) helped investigate the findings and prepare this report. The examples were rerun on CPython 3.15.2 and main, and the report received technical review. Record: [corelibs-inplace-mul-heap-left](https://github.com/Broyojo/python-formalization/blob/main/bugs/corelibs-inplace-mul-heap-left.yaml)

title: Free-threaded: pages freed by other threads are not returned while the owning thread is idle (and the default purge delay keeps them after it exits)
body:
### Bug report

In the free-threaded build (`--disable-gil`), each thread allocates from its own mimalloc heaps. When thread B frees a block owned by thread A, the block goes on the page's cross-thread free list; A collects it only when A allocates from that page, runs `mi_heap_collect`, or exits. Empty pages of QSBR-enabled heaps are not freed at once either: `_PyMem_mi_page_maybe_free()` puts them on the owner's `tstate->mimalloc.page_list`, which only the owner processes (`_PyMem_mi_heap_collect_qsbr`).

So a thread that produces data for other threads and then blocks (a worker pool, a producer, an HTTP handler thread) keeps everything it ever allocated committed. `gc.collect()` does not help: the free-threaded GC merges other threads' delayed-free queues during its stop-the-world pause (`process_delayed_frees`), but nothing collects their pages.

`main` has the same code.

#### Reproducer

Save as `idle_owner.py`. A worker thread builds N small dicts, hands the list to the main thread and blocks. The main thread drops the list and calls `gc.collect()`. Then the worker wakes, allocates a little, and later exits. The script prints RssAnon above the starting value at each step.

```python
import gc
import queue
import sys
import threading
import time

N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 300000

def rss_anon_kb():
    with open("/proc/self/status") as f:
        for line in f:
            if line.startswith("RssAnon:"):
                return int(line.split()[1])

handoff = queue.Queue()
wake = threading.Event()
done = threading.Event()

def worker():
    handoff.put([{"k": i, "v": [i, str(i)]} for i in range(N)])
    wake.wait()
    wake.clear()
    [object() for _ in range(1000)]
    done.set()
    wake.wait()

base = rss_anon_kb()
t = threading.Thread(target=worker)
t.start()
data = handoff.get()
peak = rss_anon_kb()
del data
gc.collect()
time.sleep(1)
idle = rss_anon_kb()
wake.set()
done.wait()
gc.collect()
woke = rss_anon_kb()
wake.set()
t.join()
gc.

title: /_full segment prefetch file is emitted (and ISR-rewritten) for every prerendered page even without PPR / cacheComponents
body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/Youjg25/next-full-segment-repro

### To Reproduce

1. Clone the repo, `npm install`, `npx next build` (next `16.5.0-canary.50`; same result on `16.4.2`).
2. `app/isr/page.tsx` is a plain ISR page (`export const revalidate = 60`). There is no `cacheComponents` / PPR anywhere.
3. Compare the segment output with the page RSC payload and check who can request it:

```bash
cmp .next/server/app/isr.segments/_full.segment.rsc .next/server/app/isr.rsc && echo identical   # identical
grep -c __NEXT_CLIENT_RESUME .next/server/app/isr.html   # 0 -> no client resume script
grep -rl '_full' .next/static | wc -l                     # 0 -> client router never references /_full
grep -rl '_tree' .next/static | wc -l                     # 1 -> (control) other segment names are referenced
```

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Current:** every prerendered page gets a `<page>.segments/_full.segment.rsc` file that is byte-identical to `<page>.rsc`. `collectSegmentData` sets it unconditionally (`resultMap.set('/_full', fullPageDataBuffer)` in `dist/server/app-render/collect-segment-data.js`), at build time and on every ISR revalidation.

As far as I can tell the only consumer of `/_full` is the client resume script (`createClientResumeScriptInsertionTransformStream` in `stream-utils/node-web-streams-helper.js`), which is only inserted by `continueStaticFallbackPrerender`, i.e. for static fallback shells with `fallbackRouteParams` (PPR / `cacheComponents`). The client router (`client/components/segment-cache/*`) never requests `/_full`, and without `cacheComponents` no HTML contains `__NEXT_CLIENT_RESUME`.

On Vercel each segment file is its own prerender output in the page's group, so it is re-written on every ISR revalidation. In our production app (thousands of ISR pages, Vercel Observability → ISR, last 24h) the `_full` rows have **0 reads** but account for **~42% of segment write units, ~20% of all ISR write units

title: BufferedIOBase.readinto raises `TypeError` when called on a non-blocking streams block with no data
body:
### Bug report

From PEP-3116 non-blocking should return `None` in this case (https://peps.python.org/pep-3116/#non-blocking-i-o). Goal for fixing this now is to normalize what happens between `.read` and `.readinto`; `TypeError` is definitely outside of the documented behavior.

```python
import io, _pyio, os

class Reader(io.BufferedIOBase):
    def read(self, size=-1):
        return None  # non-blocking, no data available

r, w = os.pipe()
os.set_blocking(r, False)
print(io.open(r, 'rb', closefd=False).readinto(bytearray(1)))     # None
print(_pyio.open(r, 'rb', closefd=False).readinto(bytearray(1)))  # 0
Reader().readinto(bytearray(1))  # TypeError: read() should return bytes
```

This exact fix was proposed in 2015 in `nonblock-none.patch` on gh-57531, but it never landed as that touched many other broad questsions as well. gh-109523 fixed the same kind of bug in `TextIOWrapper`: a would-block read should never surface as `TypeError`.

title: Apple testbed fails to build when its path contains a space
body:
### Bug report

The iOS testbed fails to build when it is cloned to a path that contains a space. Its "Process Python libraries" build phase runs `source $PROJECT_DIR/Python.xcframework/build/utils.sh` without quotes, so the shell splits the path at the space. The tvOS, visionOS and watchOS projects have the same line, and so does the iOS project on the 3.14 and 3.15 branches.

```
$ python Platforms/Apple/testbed clone --framework Python.xcframework "<dir>/with space/tb"
$ python "<dir>/with space/tb" run -- platform
...
<dir>/with space/tb/DerivedData/.../Script-607A66552B0F061D0010BFC8.sh: line 3: <dir>/with: No such file or directory
Command PhaseScriptExecution failed with a nonzero exit code
** TEST BUILD FAILED **
```

The same clone under `<dir>/with-hyphen/tb` builds and its test passes. This was on Xcode 27.2 with the iOS 27.2 simulator, using a 3.14.10 iOS XCframework.

The unquoted path is also glob-expanded. Run on its own with `PROJECT_DIR=<dir>/run[x]`, the build phase sourced `<dir>/runx/Python.xcframework/build/utils.sh`, which existed next to it, instead of its own.

The example build phase in `Doc/using/ios.rst` and in the `utils.sh` header comment is unquoted too, and names the file `build_utils.sh`, which the XCframework does not contain.

title: asyncio: cancelling create_connection() with happy_eyeballs_delay leaks the connected socket
body:
# Bug report

### Bug description:

When `loop.create_connection()` runs with `happy_eyeballs_delay` and is cancelled after an attempt has connected but before `staggered_race()` returns, the connected socket is never closed. It is only released by the garbage collector, with a `ResourceWarning: unclosed <socket.socket ...>`.

`staggered_race()` re-raises the `CancelledError` once its tasks finish, even when one of them has already won, so the winner's result (the socket) is dropped. `create_connection()` never sees it, so nothing closes it. Without `happy_eyeballs_delay`, `_connect_sock()` closes the socket on cancellation and nothing leaks.

Reproducer (a local server; cancel after 0–7 loop iterations):

```python
import asyncio, gc, warnings

leaks = []
warnings.simplefilter("always")
warnings.showwarning = lambda message, category, *a, **k: leaks.append(message) if category is ResourceWarning else None

async def trial(port, spins, eyeballs):
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    options = {"happy_eyeballs_delay": 0.25} if eyeballs else {}
    task = loop.create_task(loop.create_connection(asyncio.Protocol, "127.0.0.1", port, **options))
    for _ in range(spins):
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
    task.cancel()
    try:
        transport, _ = await task
        transport.close()
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        pass
    await asyncio.sleep(0)

async def main(eyeballs):
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    server = await loop.create_server(asyncio.Protocol, "127.0.0.1", 0)
    port = server.sockets[0].getsockname()[1]
    for i in range(400):
        await trial(port, i % 8, eyeballs)
    server.close()

for eyeballs in (False, True):
    leaks.clear()
    asyncio.run(main(eyeballs))
    gc.collect()
    print(f"happy_eyeballs={eyeballs}: {len(leaks)} leaked sockets")
```

Output on 3.13.12 (macOS); 3.11.15 and 3.14.3 behave the same, and the code on `main` is unchanged:

```
happy_eyeballs=False: 0 leaked sockets
happy_eyeballs=True: 199 leak

title: `asyncio.gather()` records its creator instead of the actual awaiting task in the call graph
body:
### Bug report

The call graph shows who created gather(), rather than who awaits it

Repro:

```python
import asyncio


async def consume(future):
    await future


async def main():
    release = asyncio.Event()
    child = asyncio.create_task(release.wait(), name="child")
    wrapper = asyncio.gather(child)
    consumer = asyncio.create_task(consume(wrapper), name="consumer")
    await asyncio.sleep(0)

    asyncio.print_call_graph(child)

    release.set()
    await consumer


asyncio.run(main())
```

Actual:

```
* Task(name='child', id=0x1056cc7d0)
  + Call stack:
  |   File '/Users/timofeiivankov/cpython/Lib/asyncio/locks.py', line 210, in async Event.wait()
  + Awaited by:
    * Task(name='Task-1', id=0x1056cc5f0)
      + Call stack:
      |   File '/Users/timofeiivankov/cpython/repro.py', line 15, in async main()
```

The problem here that `child` is not awaited by the `main`, it's awaited by the `gather` which in his order is awaited by consumer. At the moment of the capturing call graph, no one of the tasks or futures is not awaited by `main`

Expected:

```
* Task(name='child', id=0x101b1c7d0)
  + Call stack:
  |   File '/Users/timofeiivankov/cpython/Lib/asyncio/locks.py', line 210, in async Event.wait()
  + Awaited by:
    * Future(id=0x1017b28d0)
      + Awaited by:
        * Task(name='consumer', id=0x101b003f0)
          + Call stack:
          |   File '/Users/timofeiivankov/cpython/repro.py', line 5, in async consume()
```

Proposed fix: link children to the future returned by gather() instead of the task that created it

Problem: fix can be applied, but tests for the remote_debugging will fail, i already created https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/161508 for supportig Futures here, since it will be merged to main i'll be able to work on this issue

body:
### Bug report

```# Report: Fatal Python error `_enter_buffered_busy` when a daemon thread writes to stdout during interpreter shutdown

**Environment**
- Operating system: Windows 10/11
- Python version: 3.13
- Terminal: Windows PowerShell

## Description

I reproduced a fatal interpreter shutdown error when a daemon thread continuously writes to standard output using `print()` while the main program exits.

The error is:

```text
Fatal Python error: _enter_buffered_busy:
could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'>
at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads

Python runtime state: finalizing
```

## Minimal reproducible example

```python
import threading

def escribir():
    while True:
        print("Escribiendo en consola...")

hilo = threading.Thread(target=escribir, daemon=True)
hilo.start()

print("Finalizando programa principal...")
```

## Observed behavior

The error was reproduced on Windows using Python 3.13.

The daemon thread continues writing to stdout while the main thread exits and the interpreter begins finalization.

## Additional tests

1. A daemon thread with continuous printing can trigger the fatal error.
2. A normal thread with `join()` exits successfully.
3. A daemon thread with a limited workload and `join()` exits successfully.

## Questions for CPython maintainers

- Is this behavior entirely expected when daemon threads are writing to buffered stdout during interpreter shutdown?
- Could the shutdown process handle this situation more safely?
- Is there a recommended mechanism to prevent this fatal error when background threads write to stdout?

I would appreciate clarification and recommendations.

Thank you for your work on Python.

```

title: `logging.config.listen()` enters an infinite loop when a client disconnects early
body:
### Bug report

### Bug description

`logging.config.listen()` can enter an infinite loop and consume 100% of one CPU core when a client disconnects before sending the declared payload length.

In `ConfigStreamHandler.handle()`, the receive loop does not handle EOF. When the client closes the connection, `recv()` returns `b''`, leaving the buffer length unchanged and causing the loop to run indefinitely.

###  reproducer

```python
import logging.config
import socket
import struct
import time

t = logging.config.listen(0)
t.daemon = True
t.start()
t.ready.wait()

with socket.create_connection(("localhost", t.port)) as s:
    s.sendall(struct.pack(">L", 100) + b"abc")

time.sleep(0.5)
start = time.process_time()
time.sleep(2)
print("CPU time:", time.process_time() - start)

logging.config.stopListening()
```
## Actual behavior

The request-handling thread enters an infinite loop, consuming approximately one CPU core.

body:
### Bug report

I was exploring peak RSS gaps of the free-threaded build with mimalloc v3 (https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/159718) with overnight stress tests and had a default build and a free-threaded build configured out of tree from one checkout, as a reference. The default build then fails one test every time, also when it runs alone:

```
$ ./python -m test test_capi -m test_check_interned
  File "Lib/test/test_capi/test_unicode.py", line 1896, in test_check_interned
    self.assertEqual(check_interned(s), SSTATE_INTERNED_MORTAL)
AssertionError: 2 != 1
```

It looks like an assumption of the test (added in https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/157798, also in 3.14 and 3.15) rather than a runtime bug. Main at e8c0584877 (2026-11-10) on Linux arm64, and at 7c59816cb4 (2026-11-16) on macOS arm64. An AI assistant helped with the analysis.

### What happens

Whether it fails depends on which build wrote `Lib/test/test_capi/__pycache__/test_unicode.cpython-316.pyc`:

| the `.pyc` was written by | test run by the default build | test run by the free-threaded build |
|---|---|---|
| the default build | passes | passes |
| the free-threaded build | fails | passes |

Both builds use the cache tag `cpython-316`, so they read each other's `.pyc` files. The free-threaded build interns every string constant of a code object ([`_PyCode_ShouldInternString()`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/e8c0584877e0/Objects/codeobject.c#L116-L137)), and marshal [writes](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/e8c0584877e0/Python/marshal.c#L1043-L1046) an interned string as `TYPE_INTERNED`. When the default build loads such a file, marshal [interns](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/e8c0584877e0/Python/marshal.c#L1801-L1806) every string marked that way as immortal. The test's literal `'long string unlikely to be used by Python'` is a constant of the test's own code, so it is already interned and immortal by then, and `sys.intern()` of an equal fresh string returns that

title: Android API levels are allowed to be non-integers
body:
### Bug report

`sys.getandroidapilevel()`, and the `api_level` attribute of `platform.android_ver()` both expect the Android API level to be expressed as an integer.

Prior to Android 16, this was a reasonable assumption; Google used integer versions for API levels, and when they released a point/variant version of Android (e.g., 12L or 8.1), they would increment the API level.

However, since then:
* Android 16 QPR2 uses an Android API level of `36.1` 
* Android 17 QPR1 uses an Android API level of `37.1`
* Android 17 QPR2 uses an Android API level of `37.2`

So - the documented return type of these two methods can no longer reflect the full Android API level.

body:
# Bug report

### Bug description

For a subprocess created with `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(..., stdin=PIPE)`, `proc.stdin.wait_closed()` awaits the protocol's shared `_stdin_closed` future directly. `SubprocessStreamProtocol._get_close_waiter()` returns it, and `StreamWriter.wait_closed()` awaits it without `shield()`. If the task awaiting `wait_closed()` is cancelled after `proc.stdin.close()` but before the pipe's `connection_lost` callback runs, the cancellation cancels that shared future.

When `SubprocessStreamProtocol.pipe_connection_lost(0, None)` runs later, it calls `self._stdin_closed.set_result(None)` on the already-cancelled future. The event loop then logs:

```
Exception in callback SubprocessStreamProtocol.pipe_connection_lost()
...
asyncio.exceptions.InvalidStateError: invalid state
```

`StreamReaderProtocol` guards the equivalent future for sockets (`if not self._closed.done(): ...`); `SubprocessStreamProtocol.pipe_connection_lost()` has no such check.

title: Free-threaded: `format()` with a spec doesn't scale across threads (`PyObject_Format` refcounts the shared `__format__`)
body:
## Bug report

**CPython versions:** 3.15.2 and 3.14.10, free-threading builds (uv's python-build-standalone, Clang 23.1.3), macOS arm64. `PyObject_Format` and `_PyObject_LookupSpecial` read the same on `main` today.

On the free-threaded build, `format(x, spec)` (and so `f"{x:spec}"` and `str.format` with a spec) gets slower per call as threads are added, even though each thread formats only its own objects. At 6 threads it is about as slow as on a GIL build, where threads take turns. The same loops without a spec (`str(x)`, `f"{x}"`) scale.

### Reproduction

`repro.py` (below, pure Python, no dependencies): each of N threads runs the same loop over its own ints, e.g. `for i in range(n): format(i, "08d")`. It reports ns per call per thread, median of 5 rounds.

title: `io`: `BufferedRWPair.readline()` copies the unread buffer for every line
body:
### Feature or enhancement

`BufferedRWPair` inherits `IOBase.readline()`, which calls `peek(1)` to find the newline, then `read(n)` to consume the line. In C, each peek copies all unread bytes, up to 128 KiB by default, so reading short lines copy the same bytes over and over.

The simple idea is to relay `readline()` to the pair's `BufferedReader`.

| Call and line size | main | patch | speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `readline()`, 16 B lines | 349 ns | 35.1 ns | 9.93x |
| `readline()`, 80 B lines | 700 ns | 36.2 ns | 19.33x |
| `readline()`, 1 KiB lines | 1.26 us | 95.2 ns | 13.24x |
| `readline()`, 16 KiB lines | 6.23 us | 932 ns | 6.68x |
| `readline()`, 64 KiB lines | 21.5 us | 3.18 us | 6.77x |
| `readline(65537)`, 16 B lines | 340 ns | 37.8 ns | 9.01x |
| `readline(65537)`, 80 B lines | 716 ns | 39.2 ns | 18.26x |
| `readline(65537)`, 1 KiB lines | 1.27 us | 97.8 ns | 13.03x |
| `readline(65537)`, 16 KiB lines | 6.54 us | 938 ns | 6.98x |
| `readline(65537)`, 64 KiB lines | 23.2 us | 3.23 us | 7.17x |
| `readline()`, 16 B lines, 256 B buffer | 122 ns | 37.4 ns | 3.25x |
| `readline()`, 80 B lines, 256 B buffer | 176 ns | 57.2 ns | 3.08x |

There are real users:

* [Swift's memcached client](https://github.com/openstack/swift/blob/96f4751e2838970768f894ab6881867119f16e90/swift/common/memcached.py#L151) ([`readline()`](https://github.com/openstack/swift/blob/96f4751e2838970768f894ab6881867119f16e90/swift/common/memcached.py#L414))

title: Suggest the Markdown Editor when people open Markdown as text or in the preview
body:
Many people write Markdown in the text editor or read it in the Markdown preview without knowing that the Markdown Editor exists: it shows formatted Markdown that can be edited directly. The editor type dropdown in the breadcrumbs (**Text Editor ⌄**) can already switch to it, but it is easy to overlook.

Suggest the Markdown Editor to people who have not used it yet, at the moment it is most relevant:

- when they open a Markdown file in the text editor, and
- when they open a Markdown preview, in place or to the side.

The suggestion highlights the editor type dropdown, because that is also where they can switch back, and offers **Try Editor** (reopen the file in the Markdown Editor, without changing the default editor) and **Don't Show Again**. It shows at most once, never for editors restored at startup, and not while the user is editing.

Each suggestion should be controllable by an experiment, so we can compare which one leads people who actually want the Markdown Editor to keep using it. Whether the Markdown Editor opens files in read or edit mode at first should be controllable the same way.

title: urllib.robotparser.RobotFileParser.parse() is quadratic in repeated identical "User-agent:" lines
body:
`urllib.robotparser.RobotFileParser.parse()` scales as O(N²) in the number of identical `User-agent:` lines inside a single group. When a `robots.txt` has N `User-agent:` lines with no intervening `Allow:` or `Disallow:`, the parser accumulates one `Entry` whose `useragents` list ends up with N duplicates. `_add_entry` then walks that list and from the second iteration on calls `merge_entries(self.groups[agent], entry)`; `merge_entries` is itself O(N) because it rebuilds `useragents` from the other entry's set. The product is O(N²).

Reproducer:

```python
import time
from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser

for n in (10_000, 20_000):
    body = ("User-agent: evil\n" * n) + "Disallow: /\n"
    rp = RobotFileParser()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    rp.parse(body.splitlines())
    print(n, round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 2))
```

On Python 3.14.6 / M-series arm64:

- 10 000 lines → 2.65 s
- 20 000 lines → 10.48 s
- the ratio `dt / n²` is constant at ~27 ns, confirming pure quadratic

A minimal fix is to deduplicate inside `_add_entry` so a given agent is registered at most once per call. For every input shape except "same agent repeated within one entry" the change is a no-op; for that shape it removes the redundant self-merges that caused the quadratic.

Will post a PR.

title: xmlrpc.client: quadratic memory use with nested string elements
body:
### Bug report

Filing this as a normal bug per `xmlrpc.client`'s security note.

TL;DR: `Unmarshaller.end` keeps a fragment buffer that it doesn't clear when handling nested tags, leading to quadratic memory growth:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/562f08d6910f01e98f90e589ca5ee065fcbae53e/Lib/xmlrpc/client.py#L680

This means that `loads(...)` observes duplicate values with (for example) nested `<string>` tags:

```python
from xmlrpc.client import loads

packet = (
    "<methodResponse><params><param><value>"
    "<string><string>a<![CDATA[b]]></string></string>"
    "</value></param></params></methodResponse>"
)
values, _ = loads(packet)
print(values)
```

The above prints `('ab', 'ab')` despite there being only one `ab` in the payload.

I'm pretty sure the fix for this is just:

```python
data = "".join(self._data)
self._data.clear()
return f(self, data)
```

i.e. compute the joined version and then clear the fragment buffer rather than keeping it around to grow.

One wrinkle: this _does_ change the observable outcome with the `loads(...)` API: the example above becomes `('ab', None)`. I actually think this is more correct anyways, since XML-RPC has no semantics for nested scalars like `<string>`.

title: Code blocks in chat requests leave a large gap on the right
body: Code blocks in chat **requests** (the user's message bubble) leave a large empty strip on the right: the editor ends well before the code block's border, so long lines get cut off even though there is free space. It happens in both the Agents window and the editor window chat, in light and dark themes. | 1 | 2 | |---|---| | | | Steps to reproduce: 1. Send a chat message that contains a fenced code block with long lines. 2. Look at the code block in your request bubble: there is a gap between the end of the editor and the right border of the code block. Cause: `CodeBlockPart.layout` sizes the editor of request code blocks at a hard-coded `0.9 × width` of the chat list, but the request bubble's width is decided by CSS, with a different max-width in each context: 90% in the editor window, 100% in the Agents window when the bubble contains a code block, and 85% on mobile. Because the two don't match, the editor is narrower than its container. Proposed fix: lay out request code block editors to the measured width of their container (with a `ResizeObserver`), and make request bubbles that contain a code block fill their max-width so the bubble doesn't size itself to the editor. 🤖 Authored with GitHub Copilot on behalf of @alexdima.

title: Sessions: per-session policy config reads deep-clone the full configuration; each agent-host notification blocks the renderer up to ~1.6 s
body:
**Version:** 1.147.0 stable (`8a14f0cc1b08d531eb83255ea3764ae22aa932b5`) · Windows 11. The Copilot account's policy disables the local Claude and Codex harnesses: `inspect(...).policyValue === false` for both `chat.agentHost.claudeAgent.enabled` and `chat.agentHost.codexAgent.enabled`.

## Symptoms
In the Agents window, the renderer main thread sits at ~100% while agent-host sessions are active. Scrolling and animations are janky, and New Session takes ~4.4 s to become usable.

## Repro
1. Use an account whose policy disables the Claude/Codex local harnesses (above).
2. Have Claude or Codex sessions in the sessions cache, e.g. external Claude Code sessions listed via `chat.agentSessions.showExternal: "last30Days"`. Here: 25 Claude + 6 Codex out of 169.
3. Open the Agents window, then let a session stream or click New Session.
4. Profile the renderer.

## Root cause
Renderer profile while saturated (10.9 s): **85% in `Configuration.getConsolidatedConfigurationModel`** (84% self time in `deepClone`), 0.1% idle. A single agent-host notification blocks the main thread for **1.0–1.6 s**.

```
agent-host notification (isRead / session state / summary changed) → onDidChangeSessions
 ├─ title-bar command center → getRecentlyOpenedSessions → 10× getSession   (~32%)
 ├─ customizations / MCP target resolution → getSession                     (~25%)
 └─ sessions list, default placement, turn pills, …                         (rest)
    → SessionsManagementService.getSession → _getAllSessions()   (every provider, every lookup)
    → BaseAgentHostSessionsProvider.getAllSessions()             (policy gate per cached session)
    → configurationService.getValue / inspect(policy-managed key)
    → getConsolidatedConfigurationModel → ConfigurationModel.merge() → deepClone(entire config)
```

1. **Platform:** [`configurationModels.ts#L1068-L1074`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/8a14f0cc1b08d531eb83255ea3764ae22aa932b5/src/vs/platform/configuration/common/configurationModels.t
